objectives: Students will describe the states of matter and phase changes in terms of particle motion.
Students will use atomic number, mass number, and the periodic table to describe atoms and predict which elements behave alike.

teach:
Week 7 Science: Chemistry — Matter, Atoms, the Periodic Table, Reactions, Solutions, and pH

Objectives

  • Describe solids, liquids, and gases in terms of particle motion and spacing, and name the phase changes.
  • Use atomic number and mass number to find the protons, neutrons, and electrons in an atom, and use the periodic table to predict which elements behave alike.
  • Classify matter as an element, compound, or mixture, and classify changes as physical or chemical.
  • Balance simple chemical equations and apply the law of conservation of mass.
  • Calculate density and concentration, read solubility tables, and interpret the pH scale.

Materials

  • Whiteboard or shared screen; markers in three colors.
  • A simple periodic table (one per student, printed or on screen).
  • Calculator for each student (the GED Science test provides an on-screen calculator).
  • This week's Student Lesson, Study Notes, and the 12 practice items on the course page.

60-Minute Timing Plan

SegmentMinutesWhat happens
Warm-up5Physical or chemical? Sort six everyday changes.
Direct instruction20States of matter, atoms, periodic table, elements and compounds, reactions and balancing, conservation of mass, density, solutions, pH; Worked Examples 1–4.
Guided practice15The propane grill problem: balance, classify, apply conservation of mass, compute concentration.
Independent practice15Practice items 1–12 on the course page (finish for homework if needed).
Wrap-up5Checks for understanding; preview the exit ticket, study plan, and this week's Practice GED.

This is a content-heavy week. If time runs short, prioritize balancing equations, conservation of mass, and reading data tables (solubility, density, pH). Those three skills produce the most GED points. States of matter and the atom can be reviewed quickly because most students have seen them before.

Warm-up (5 minutes)

Write these six changes on the board and ask students to label each one P (physical change) or C (chemical change):

  1. A puddle dries up on a sunny day.
  2. A cake bakes in the oven.
  3. A glass bottle shatters.
  4. A match burns.
  5. Butter melts in a hot pan.
  6. An antacid tablet fizzes in water.

Answers: 1 P, 2 C, 3 P, 4 C, 5 P, 6 C.

Ask: "What do the C answers have in common?" Expected answer: a new substance forms (new gas bubbles, light and heat, a change that cannot be undone). The P answers change only form or state.

Direct Instruction (20 minutes) — Talking Points

1. Matter and its states. Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. All matter is made of tiny particles that are always moving.

StateShapeVolumeParticles
SolidDefiniteDefinitePacked tightly; vibrate in place
LiquidTakes the shape of its containerDefiniteClose together; slide past one another
GasFills its containerFills its containerFar apart; move fast in all directions

Adding heat speeds particles up: melting, evaporation/boiling, and sublimation (solid straight to gas, like dry ice). Removing heat reverses these: freezing and condensation. During melting or boiling, temperature stays constant (the flat parts of a heating graph).

2. The atom. An atom is the smallest unit of an element that keeps that element's identity.

  • Protons: positive charge, in the nucleus.
  • Neutrons: no charge, in the nucleus.
  • Electrons: negative charge, moving around the nucleus; very little mass.

Atomic number = number of protons (this defines the element).
Mass number = protons + neutrons.
Neutrons = mass number − atomic number.
In a neutral atom, electrons = protons.

Mention briefly: isotopes are atoms of one element with different numbers of neutrons (carbon-12, carbon-14); an atom that gains or loses electrons is a charged ion.

3. The periodic table. Elements are arranged in order of atomic number. Rows are periods; columns are groups. Elements in the same group have similar chemical properties because they have the same number of outer (valence) electrons. Metals are on the left, nonmetals on the right. Group 1 metals (lithium, sodium, potassium) react strongly with water; Group 18 noble gases rarely react.

4. Elements, compounds, and mixtures.

  • Element: only one kind of atom (iron, Fe; oxygen gas, O2).
  • Compound: two or more elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio (water, H2O; table salt, NaCl). Its properties can differ greatly from its elements: sodium and chlorine are dangerous alone, but NaCl is table salt.
  • Mixture: substances physically combined, not bonded, in any ratio (salt water, air, trail mix). Mixtures can be separated by physical means such as filtering or evaporation.

Teach students to read a formula: in H2O, the subscript 2 means two hydrogen atoms; no subscript means one, so there is one oxygen atom.

5. Physical vs. chemical changes. A physical change alters form or state but not identity (cutting, melting, dissolving, boiling). A chemical change (chemical reaction) makes new substances. Evidence of a chemical change: a gas forms (bubbles), a color change, light or heat is given off or absorbed, a solid (precipitate) forms when two liquids are mixed, or a new odor appears.

6. Chemical equations and conservation of mass. In a chemical equation, reactants are on the left of the arrow and products are on the right. The law of conservation of mass says that matter is not created or destroyed in a chemical reaction. Atoms are only rearranged, so the total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products. That is why equations must be balanced: the same number of each kind of atom on both sides.

Balancing method: (1) Count each kind of atom on each side. (2) Change only coefficients (the big numbers in front), never subscripts. (3) Balance elements that appear in only one substance on each side first; save hydrogen and oxygen (or a lone element like O2) for last. (4) Recount everything. (5) Use the smallest whole numbers.

Why subscripts are locked: H2O2 is hydrogen peroxide, not water.

Worked Example 1: Burning natural gas. Balance: CH4 + O2 → CO2 + H2O

Step 1, count. Left: C 1, H 4, O 2. Right: C 1, H 2, O 3 (2 in CO2 + 1 in H2O).

Step 2, carbon is already balanced (1 and 1).

Step 3, hydrogen: 4 on the left, 2 on the right. Put a 2 in front of H2O: CH4 + O2 → CO2 + 2H2O. Now H is 4 and 4.

Step 4, oxygen: right side now has 2 + 2(1) = 4. Left has 2. Put a 2 in front of O2: 2 × 2 = 4.

Recount: C 1 = 1; H 4 = 4; O 4 = 4.

Answer: CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O (coefficients 1, 2, 1, 2).

Worked Example 2: Rust. Balance: Fe + O2 → Fe2O3

Count. Left: Fe 1, O 2. Right: Fe 2, O 3.

Oxygen is the hard part: 2 on the left and 3 on the right. The smallest number both 2 and 3 divide into is 6. To get 6 on the left, use 3O2 (3 × 2 = 6). To get 6 on the right, use 2Fe2O3 (2 × 3 = 6).

Now iron: right side has 2 × 2 = 4 Fe, so put 4 in front of Fe.

Recount: Fe 4 = 4; O 6 = 6.

Answer: 4Fe + 3O2 → 2Fe2O3. This "least common multiple" move handles odd-and-even oxygen counts.

7. Conservation of mass in the lab. When lab mass seems to drop, ask: "Was the container open?" A gas product escapes an open container unweighed; in a sealed container, total mass stays the same. Burning steel wool in open air gains mass, because it combines with oxygen that was never weighed.

8. Density. Density is mass per unit volume: D = m ÷ V, usually in g/mL or g/cm3 (1 mL = 1 cm3). Density helps identify an unknown substance. Water is 1.00 g/mL; less dense objects float, denser ones sink. For an irregular solid, use water displacement: volume = final level − starting level.

Worked Example 3: Identify a metal. A metal bolt has a mass of 78.7 g. A graduated cylinder holds 40.0 mL of water; after the bolt is added, the level is 50.0 mL. Known densities (g/cm3): aluminum 2.70, titanium 4.51, iron 7.87, silver 10.5.

Volume = 50.0 mL − 40.0 mL = 10.0 mL = 10.0 cm3.

Density = 78.7 g ÷ 10.0 cm3 = 7.87 g/cm3.

Answer: The bolt is most likely iron. It would sink in water because 7.87 > 1.00. Common error: dividing by 50.0 mL (the final level) instead of the change, which gives 1.57 g/cm3.

9. Solutions, concentration, and solubility. In a solution, a solute (sugar) is spread evenly through a solvent (water). Concentration (g/L) = grams of solute ÷ liters of solution. Adding water dilutes: the solute stays the same, the volume grows, the concentration falls.

Solubility is the most solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a given temperature (often g per 100 g of water). At that limit the solution is saturated. Most solids dissolve more when warmer; gases dissolve less (warm soda goes flat). Cooling a solution below its limit makes the extra solute crystallize.

Worked Example 4: Reading a solubility table. The solubility of potassium chloride is about 51 g per 100 g of water at 80 °C and about 34 g per 100 g of water at 20 °C. A student dissolves 50 g of potassium chloride in 100 g of water at 80 °C, then cools the solution to 20 °C. How many grams of solid come out of solution?

At 80 °C, 50 g < 51 g, so all 50 g dissolves (the solution is unsaturated).

At 20 °C, only 34 g can stay dissolved.

Solid that comes out = 50 g − 34 g = 16 g.

Common error: subtracting the two solubilities (51 − 34 = 17 g). That would only be right if the solution had been fully saturated at 80 °C. Always start from the amount actually dissolved.

10. Acids, bases, and pH. The pH scale runs from 0 to 14: below 7 is acidic (sour; lemon juice, vinegar), 7 is neutral (pure water), above 7 is basic (bitter, slippery; baking soda, ammonia). The key GED fact: each pH unit is a factor of 10. Tomato juice (pH 4) is 10 × 10 = 100 times more acidic than milk (pH 6), not 2 or 20 times. An acid and a base neutralize each other, moving the pH toward 7.

Guided Practice (15 minutes)

Work through this together; let students try each step before revealing it.

A backyard grill burns propane gas, C3H8. The unbalanced equation is C3H8 + O2 → CO2 + H2O.

  1. Balance the equation.
  2. Is burning propane a physical or a chemical change? Give two pieces of evidence.
  3. In one test, 44 g of propane reacts completely with 160 g of oxygen. What is the total mass of the products?
  4. Separately, a cleaning solution is made by dissolving 10 g of baking soda in enough water to make 250 mL of solution. What is its concentration in g/L? Would its pH be above or below 7?

1. Carbon: 3 on the left, so 3CO2. Hydrogen: 8 on the left, so 4H2O (4 × 2 = 8). Oxygen on the right: 3(2) + 4(1) = 6 + 4 = 10, so 5O2 (5 × 2 = 10). C3H8 + 5O2 → 3CO2 + 4H2O. Recount: C 3 = 3, H 8 = 8, O 10 = 10.

2. Chemical. New substances (carbon dioxide and water) form, and heat and light are given off.

3. By conservation of mass, products = reactants = 44 g + 160 g = 204 g.

4. 250 mL = 0.250 L. Concentration = 10 g ÷ 0.250 L = 40 g/L. Baking soda is a base, so the pH is above 7.

Checks for Understanding

  • "An atom has atomic number 20 and mass number 40. How many neutrons?" Expected: 40 − 20 = 20.
  • "Why can't we balance H2 + O2 → H2O by writing H2O2?" Expected: changing a subscript makes a different substance (hydrogen peroxide); only coefficients may change. Correct balance: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O.
  • "A block has a density of 0.8 g/cm3. Will it float in water?" Expected: yes, because 0.8 < 1.00.
  • "A solution has pH 9. Is it acidic, neutral, or basic?" Expected: basic.

Common Mistakes and How to Correct Them

Changing subscripts to balance. Correction: circle subscripts first and call them "locked."

Forgetting a coefficient multiplies every atom. 2H2O has 4 H and 2 O, not 4 and 1. Correction: write the multiplication out (2 × 2 = 4 H; 2 × 1 = 2 O).

Thinking mass is "lost" when a gas forms. Correction: ask whether the container was open; the "lost" mass left as gas.

Treating pH as ordinary subtraction. Correction: write 10(difference); 3 units = 103 = 1,000 times.

Using the final water level as the volume, or calling dissolving a chemical change. Correction: volume = final − starting level; dissolved sugar is still sugar (a physical change).

Differentiation

Support: Provide an atom-counting chart (elements down the side, "Left" and "Right" columns) and colored paper squares to model atoms. Give the density triangle (m on top, D and V below) and a pH "powers of 10" card.

Stretch: Balance C2H6 + O2 → CO2 + H2O (answer: 2C2H6 + 7O2 → 4CO2 + 6H2O; C 4 = 4, H 12 = 12, O 14 = 8 + 6). Explain with particle motion why warm soda goes flat faster.

How This Shows Up on the GED

GED chemistry questions usually come with a short description, table, or graph and ask students to apply a rule (conservation of mass, D = m ÷ V, the pH scale) rather than recall facts. Expect wording like:

  • "Which coefficients balance the equation?" (often drop-down menus in front of each formula)
  • "Based on the table, at what temperature…?" or "How many grams of solute will crystallize…?"
  • "Which statement best explains why the mass of the flask decreased?"
  • "What is the density of the sample?" (fill-in-the-blank with units given)
  • "How many times more acidic…?"
  • "Which change is a chemical change?" or drag-and-drop sorting of changes or substances.

The on-screen calculator is available throughout the Science test, so emphasize correct setup over hand arithmetic.

Wrap-up (5 minutes)

Run the checks for understanding, then preview the exit ticket, the study plan, and this week's Practice GED.
student:
Chemistry: Matter, Atoms, Reactions, Solutions, and pH

Chemistry is the study of matter and how it changes. On the GED Science test, chemistry questions usually give you a table, a graph, or a short lab description and ask you to apply a few key rules. This lesson gives you those rules and shows you how to use them.

1. States of matter

Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. It is made of tiny particles that are always moving.

  • Solid: definite shape and volume; particles packed tightly, vibrating in place.
  • Liquid: definite volume but takes the shape of its container; particles close but sliding past one another.
  • Gas: no definite shape or volume; particles far apart and moving fast.

Adding heat speeds particles up: solids melt, liquids evaporate or boil. Removing heat slows them down: gases condense, liquids freeze. While something is melting or boiling, its temperature stays the same until the change is finished.

2. Atoms and the periodic table

Everything is built from atoms. Each atom has a center called the nucleus holding protons (positive) and neutrons (no charge). Electrons (negative) move around the nucleus.

Atomic number = protons
Mass number = protons + neutrons
Neutrons = mass number − atomic number
Neutral atom: electrons = protons

The periodic table lists the elements in order of atomic number. The columns are called groups. Elements in the same group act alike. For example, sodium and potassium are both in Group 1, and both react strongly with water. Metals are on the left side of the table and nonmetals are on the right.

3. Elements, compounds, and mixtures

  • An element has only one kind of atom: gold (Au), oxygen gas (O2).
  • A compound is two or more elements chemically joined in a fixed ratio: water (H2O), carbon dioxide (CO2).
  • A mixture is substances mixed together but not chemically joined: salt water, air, a salad.

In a chemical formula, the small number written low, called a subscript, tells how many of the atom before it. CO2 has 1 carbon atom and 2 oxygen atoms.

4. Physical and chemical changes

A physical change changes the size, shape, or state, but the substance is still the same: melting ice, chopping wood, dissolving sugar. A chemical change makes a new substance: burning wood, rusting iron, baking bread. Signs of a chemical change include bubbles of a new gas, a color change, heat or light given off, or a new solid forming.

5. Chemical equations and conservation of mass

A chemical equation shows a reaction. Reactants (starting substances) are on the left of the arrow; products (new substances) are on the right.

The law of conservation of mass says matter is not created or destroyed in a reaction. The atoms just rearrange. So the total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products, and an equation must be balanced: the same number of each kind of atom on both sides.

How to balance: Count atoms on each side. Change only the big numbers in front, called coefficients. Never change the subscripts. Recount after each change. A coefficient multiplies every atom in that formula: 3H2O has 3 × 2 = 6 H atoms and 3 × 1 = 3 O atoms.

Example 1. Balance N2 + H2 → NH3 (making ammonia).

Count: Left N 2, H 2. Right N 1, H 3.

Nitrogen: put 2 in front of NH3. Now the right has N 2 and H 2 × 3 = 6.

Hydrogen: the left needs 6, so put 3 in front of H2 (3 × 2 = 6).

Check: N 2 = 2, H 6 = 6. N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3

If a reaction makes a gas in an open container, the mass on the scale goes down because the gas escapes into the air. The mass was not destroyed. In a sealed container, the mass stays the same.

6. Density

Density is how much mass is packed into a certain volume.

Density = mass ÷ volume   (D = m ÷ V)

Units: g/mL or g/cm3 (1 mL = 1 cm3). Water = 1.00 g/mL.

An object less dense than water floats; one more dense sinks. To find the volume of an odd-shaped object, drop it in a graduated cylinder of water. Its volume is the rise in the water level.

Example 2. A stone has a mass of 63 g. The water level rises from 30 mL to 51 mL when it is added. Find its density. Will it float?

Volume = 51 mL − 30 mL = 21 mL

Density = 63 g ÷ 21 mL = 3 g/mL

3 is greater than 1.00, so the stone sinks.

7. Solutions and concentration

A solution is an even mixture. The solute is what dissolves (salt); the solvent does the dissolving (water). Concentration is how much solute is in a certain amount of solution.

Concentration (g/L) = grams of solute ÷ liters of solution

Solubility is the most solute that can dissolve in a certain amount of solvent at a given temperature. A solution holding that much is saturated. Most solids dissolve better in hot water. Gases do the opposite: they dissolve better in cold liquid. If you cool a solution, any solute above the new limit comes out as solid crystals.

Example 3. A sports drink has 24 g of sugar in 400 mL of drink. What is the sugar concentration in g/L?

400 mL = 0.400 L

Concentration = 24 g ÷ 0.400 L = 60 g/L

8. Acids, bases, and pH

The pH scale goes from 0 to 14.

pHTypeEveryday examples
Below 7Acid (sour)Lemon juice, vinegar, soda
7NeutralPure water
Above 7Base (bitter, slippery)Baking soda, soap, ammonia

The lower the pH, the stronger the acid. The higher the pH, the stronger the base. Each step of 1 pH unit means 10 times stronger. When an acid and a base mix, they neutralize each other and the pH moves toward 7.

Example 4. Rainwater in one area has pH 5. Stream water nearby has pH 7. How many times more acidic is the rainwater?

Difference = 7 − 5 = 2 units

10 × 10 = 100 times more acidic

Try It

1. Chlorine has atomic number 17. A chlorine atom has mass number 35. How many neutrons does it have? How many electrons does a neutral chlorine atom have?

Show answer

Neutrons = 35 − 17 = 18. A neutral atom has as many electrons as protons, so it has 17 electrons.

2. Balance: Mg + O2 → MgO

Show answer

Oxygen: 2 on the left, 1 on the right, so write 2MgO. Now magnesium is 2 on the right, so write 2Mg. 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO. Check: Mg 2 = 2, O 2 = 2.

3. A plastic block has a mass of 30 g and a volume of 40 cm3. What is its density? Will it float in water?

Show answer

D = 30 ÷ 40 = 0.75 g/cm3. Since 0.75 < 1.00, it floats.

4. A nurse dissolves 18 g of salt in enough water to make 2.0 L of solution. What is the concentration in g/L?

Show answer

18 g ÷ 2.0 L = 9 g/L.

5. Is frying an egg a physical change or a chemical change? Explain.

Show answer

Chemical change. The egg changes color and texture, and the cooked egg is a new substance that cannot be turned back into a raw egg.
post:
Post Lesson: Chemistry

Summary of Key Points

  • Solids have a definite shape and volume, liquids have a definite volume only, and gases have neither. Adding heat speeds particles up and can change the state.
  • Atomic number = protons. Mass number = protons + neutrons. In a neutral atom, electrons = protons. Elements in the same group of the periodic table behave alike.
  • Elements have one kind of atom; compounds are elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio; mixtures are not bonded and can be separated physically.
  • Physical changes keep the same substance; chemical changes make new substances (gas, color change, heat or light, new solid).
  • Mass is conserved in every reaction. Balance equations by changing coefficients only, never subscripts.
  • Density = mass ÷ volume. Less dense than water (1.00 g/mL) floats.
  • Concentration = solute ÷ solution volume. Most solids dissolve better when warmer; gases dissolve better when colder.
  • pH below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, above 7 is basic. Each pH unit is a factor of 10.

Exit Ticket

1. An atom has 26 protons and 30 neutrons. What is its mass number?

Show answer

26 + 30 = 56. (This is iron-56.)

2. Balance: Na + Cl2 → NaCl

Show answer

2Na + Cl2 → 2NaCl. Check: Na 2 = 2, Cl 2 = 2.

3. A candle burns on a scale in an open room, and the reading goes down. Has mass been destroyed? Explain.

Show answer

No. The wax reacts with oxygen to make carbon dioxide and water vapor, which are gases that drift away and are not weighed. If everything were trapped in a sealed container, the total mass would not change.

4. A 12.0 g sample has a volume of 4.0 mL. What is its density?

Show answer

12.0 ÷ 4.0 = 3.0 g/mL.

5. Solution A has pH 2 and Solution B has pH 5. Which is more acidic, and by what factor?

Show answer

Solution A, by 103 = 1,000 times (5 − 2 = 3 units).

Reflection

  • Which skill this week felt most comfortable (balancing, density, concentration, or pH), and which one do you want more practice with?
  • Name two chemical changes and two physical changes you saw at home or at work this week. What evidence told you which was which?
  • In your own words, explain why a coefficient can change but a subscript cannot.

This Week's Study Plan (20–40 minutes a day)

DayTask
Day 1Reread the Student Lesson. Redo the Try It problems without looking. Make a card with the atom, density, concentration, and pH rules. (25 min)
Day 2Balancing practice: rebalance every equation in the lesson from scratch, counting atoms in a chart. Do practice items 1–6. (30 min)
Day 3Do practice items 7–12. For each item you miss, read the explanation and write one sentence about the step you skipped. (30 min)
Day 4Study the vocabulary until you can define each term from memory. Reread the Study Notes and quiz yourself on the pH and density rules. (25 min)
Day 5Take this week's Practice GED in one sitting with the timer on. (90 min, may be split over two days)
Day 6Review every Practice GED question you missed. Sort your mistakes by type (reading the data, the science rule, or arithmetic) and reread that part of the lesson. (30–40 min)

Test-Taking Strategy: Make an Atom Chart

When a question asks you to balance an equation, do not guess coefficients in your head. On your scratch paper, write each element down the side and two columns labeled "Left" and "Right." Fill in the counts, change one coefficient, and update the chart. Before you submit, check that every row matches. This takes less than a minute and catches the most common error: forgetting that a coefficient multiplies every atom in a formula.

The number of protons in an atom; it decides which element the atom is.
vocab.example: Oxygen's atomic number is 8, so every oxygen atom has 8 protons.

vocab.def: The total number of protons and neutrons in an atom's nucleus.
vocab.example: Carbon-14 has 6 protons and 8 neutrons, so its mass number is 14.

vocab.def: A pure substance made of only one kind of atom.

vocab.example: Water, H<sub>2</sub>O, always has two hydrogen atoms for every oxygen atom.

vocab.def: Two or more substances combined without bonding; they can be separated by physical means.
vocab.example: Sand and iron filings can be separated with a magnet.

vocab.def: A change that produces one or more new substances.
A change in size, shape, or state that does not make a new substance.

vocab.example: 10 g of reactants always make 10 g of products.

vocab.example: 5 g of sugar in 1 L of tea is a concentration of 5 g/L.

notes:
Study Notes: Chemistry

States of Matter

Solid: fixed shape and volume. Liquid: fixed volume. Gas: neither.
Add heat: melt, evaporate/boil, sublimate. Remove heat: freeze, condense.
Temperature stays flat during a phase change.

The Atom

Atomic number = protons
Mass number = protons + neutrons
Neutrons = mass # − atomic #
Neutral atom: electrons = protons

Periodic table: columns = groups (similar properties); rows = periods. Metals left, nonmetals right, noble gases far right (Group 18).

Element / Compound / Mixture

Element: one kind of atom (Fe, O2).
Compound: bonded, fixed ratio (H2O, NaCl).
Mixture: not bonded, separable (salt water, air).

Changes

Physical: same substance (melt, cut, dissolve).
Chemical: new substance. Clues: gas, color change, heat/light, new solid.

Balancing Equations

  1. Count atoms on each side.
  2. Change coefficients only, never subscripts.
  3. Coefficient × subscript = atoms (3H2O: 6 H, 3 O).
  4. Recount; use smallest whole numbers.

Conservation of mass: mass of reactants = mass of products. Open container + gas made = mass seems to drop.

Formulas

Density = mass ÷ volume (water = 1.00 g/mL)
Displacement volume = final − starting level
Concentration (g/L) = g solute ÷ L solution

pH0–678–14
TypeAcid (sour; blue litmus turns red)Neutral (pure water)Base (bitter, slippery; red litmus turns blue)
ExamplesLemon juice 2, vinegar 3Water 7Baking soda 9, ammonia 11

pH rule: 1 unit = 10 times; 2 units = 100 times; 3 units = 1,000 times. Solubility: most solids dissolve more in warm water; gases dissolve more in cold. Cooling a solution below its limit makes crystals: amount out = amount dissolved − new limit.

stimuli.html:
When baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) is mixed with vinegar (acetic acid), the mixture fizzes. The reaction is:

NaHCO3 + CH3COOH → CH3COONa + H2O + CO2

A student ran this reaction two ways.

Trial 1 (open): She placed a flask of vinegar and a small cup of baking soda together on a balance and recorded the total mass. She poured the baking soda into the flask, left the flask open, waited until the fizzing stopped, and placed the flask and empty cup back on the balance.

Trial 2 (sealed): She put vinegar in a plastic bottle and lowered a small tube of baking soda inside without letting them touch. She screwed the cap on tightly and recorded the total mass. Then she tipped the bottle so the substances mixed, waited until the fizzing stopped, and recorded the mass again without opening the bottle.

TrialTotal mass before (g)Total mass after (g)

stimuli.title: pH of Household Substances
stimuli.html:
A student used a pH meter to test several substances found at home. The results are shown in the table.

SubstancepH
Lemon juice2
Vinegar3
Black coffee5
Distilled water7
Baking soda solution9
Ammonia cleaner11

items.prompt: A substance has no definite shape and no definite volume. Its particles are far apart and move quickly in all directions. In which state of matter is this substance?
items.hint: Which state spreads out to fill any container it is in?
items.explain:
A gas has no definite shape or volume; it spreads out to fill its container because its particles are far apart and moving fast.

A liquid has a definite volume (it only takes the shape of its container), so it does not fit. A solid has both a definite shape and a definite volume. A crystal is a type of solid, with particles locked in a regular pattern.

items.prompt: Sodium has an atomic number of 11. A neutral sodium atom has a mass number of 23. Which choice correctly describes this atom?
items.hint: Atomic number tells you the protons. Subtract it from the mass number to get the neutrons.
items.explain:
Protons = atomic number = 11.

Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 23 − 11 = 12.

In a neutral atom, electrons = protons = 11.

The choice with 23 protons uses the mass number as the proton count, which is a common error. The choice with 12 electrons would describe a charged ion, not a neutral atom.

items.prompt: Sort each change into the correct category.
choices: Ice cream melting on a hot day
items.hint: Ask: is a new substance formed, or is it still the same substance in a different form?
items.explain:
Physical changes (same substance, new form or state): melting ice cream, tearing paper, and dissolving sugar. The dissolved sugar is still sugar and could be recovered by evaporating the water.

Chemical changes (new substances form): rusting (iron combines with oxygen to form iron oxide), burning wood (forms ash, carbon dioxide, and water vapor and gives off heat and light), and souring milk (bacteria produce acid, which changes the taste and texture).

items.prompt: Based on the data, the solubility of which salt is least affected by a change in temperature?
options: All three salts are affected equally.
items.hint: For each salt, compare its value at 0 °C with its value at 80 °C.
items.explain:
Change in solubility from 0 °C to 80 °C:

  • Sodium chloride: 38 − 36 = 2 g
  • Potassium chloride: 51 − 28 = 23 g
  • Potassium nitrate: 169 − 13 = 156 g

Sodium chloride changes the least; its line on the graph is nearly flat. Potassium nitrate is the most affected, which is the opposite of what the question asks.

items.prompt: A student dissolves 100 g of potassium nitrate in 100 g of water at 60 °C. She then cools the solution to 20 °C. About how many grams of potassium nitrate will come out of the solution as solid crystals?
items.hint: First check whether all 100 g dissolved at 60 °C. Then find how much can stay dissolved at 20 °C.
items.explain:
At 60 °C, up to 110 g can dissolve in 100 g of water. Since 100 g < 110 g, all 100 g dissolves.

At 20 °C, only 32 g can stay dissolved.

Crystals formed = 100 g − 32 g = 68 g.

78 g comes from subtracting the two solubilities (110 − 32), but the student dissolved only 100 g, not 110 g. 32 g is the amount that stays dissolved, not the amount that comes out.

items.prompt: What is the density of Sample A? Round to the nearest hundredth.
items.hint: The sample's volume is the change in the water level. Then divide mass by volume.
items.explain:
Volume of Sample A = 70.0 mL − 50.0 mL = 20.0 mL.

Density = mass ÷ volume = 54.0 g ÷ 20.0 mL = 2.70 g/mL.

A common error is dividing by the final water level: 54.0 ÷ 70.0 ≈ 0.77 g/mL. The volume of the sample is only the rise in the water level. The correct value, 2.70 g/mL, matches aluminum in the reference table.

items.prompt: Based on its density, Sample B is most likely made of which metal?
items.hint: Find Sample B's volume from the water levels, calculate its density, and match it to the reference table.
items.explain:
Volume of Sample B = 50.0 mL − 40.0 mL = 10.0 mL = 10.0 cm3.

Density = 89.6 g ÷ 10.0 cm3 = 8.96 g/cm3, which matches copper.

Zinc (7.14) is the density of Sample C: 71.4 ÷ 10.0 = 7.14. Lead (11.3) matches Sample D: 56.5 ÷ 5.0 = 11.3. Choosing the metal with the largest mass or the largest density value without calculating leads to the wrong answer.

items.prompt:
Hydrogen gas burns in oxygen to form water. Choose the coefficients that balance the equation using the smallest whole numbers. (A coefficient of 1 is shown here, although it is usually left unwritten.)

{{0}} H2 + {{1}} O2 → {{2}} H2O
items.hint: Balance oxygen first: O<sub>2</sub> has 2 oxygen atoms, but each H<sub>2</sub>O has only 1.
items.explain:
Unbalanced count: left H 2, O 2; right H 2, O 1.

Oxygen: put 2 in front of H2O, giving O 2 on the right. Now hydrogen on the right is 2 × 2 = 4.

Hydrogen: put 2 in front of H2, giving 2 × 2 = 4 on the left.

Check: H 4 = 4; O 2 = 2. 2H2 + 1O2 → 2H2O, written as 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O.

Choosing 1, 1, 1 leaves oxygen unbalanced (2 on the left, 1 on the right). You cannot fix it by changing H2O to H2O2, because that would make a different substance.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains why the total mass decreased in Trial 1 but not in Trial 2?
options: In Trial 1, carbon dioxide gas escaped into the air and was not weighed; in Trial 2, the gas was trapped inside the bottle.
In Trial 1, about 1.10 g of matter was destroyed by the reaction; in Trial 2, the cap prevented the reaction from destroying matter.
In Trial 1, the reaction did not follow the law of conservation of mass because the flask was made of glass.
In Trial 2, the baking soda and vinegar did not react, so no mass was lost.
items.hint: Look at the products in the equation. Which one is a gas? Where could it go in an open flask?
items.explain:
One product of the reaction is carbon dioxide (CO2), a gas. In the open flask of Trial 1, the gas bubbled out into the room, so the balance did not weigh it. The mass of the escaped gas is 182.40 g − 181.30 g = 1.10 g.

In the sealed bottle of Trial 2, all products, including the gas, stayed inside, so the total mass stayed at 183.10 g. This supports the law of conservation of mass.

Matter is never destroyed in a chemical reaction, so the choice that says 1.10 g was destroyed is wrong. The fizzing described in Trial 2 shows that a reaction did happen there.

items.prompt:
When aluminum metal is exposed to oxygen, it forms a thin coating of aluminum oxide. Choose the coefficients that balance the equation using the smallest whole numbers.

{{0}} Al + {{1}} O2 → {{2}} Al2O3
items.hint: Oxygen comes in 2s on the left and 3s on the right. What is the smallest number that both 2 and 3 divide into evenly?
items.explain:
Unbalanced count: left Al 1, O 2; right Al 2, O 3.

Oxygen: the least common multiple of 2 and 3 is 6. Use 3O2 (3 × 2 = 6) and 2Al2O3 (2 × 3 = 6).

Aluminum: the right side now has 2 × 2 = 4 Al, so use 4Al on the left.

Check: Al 4 = 4; O 6 = 6. 4Al + 3O2 → 2Al2O3.

A common wrong answer is 2Al + O2 → Al2O3; it balances aluminum (2 = 2) but leaves oxygen at 2 on the left and 3 on the right.

items.prompt: Based on the table, which two statements are correct? Select two answers.
options: Lemon juice is 10 times more acidic than vinegar.
Black coffee is a base because its pH is closer to 7 than vinegar's pH is.
Distilled water is the most acidic substance in the table.
Baking soda solution is an acid because its pH is a single-digit number.
items.hint: pH below 7 is acidic and above 7 is basic. Each 1-unit difference in pH is a factor of 10.
items.explain:
Correct: Lemon juice (pH 2) and vinegar (pH 3) differ by 1 unit, and each unit is a factor of 10, so lemon juice is 10 times more acidic. Ammonia cleaner has a pH of 11, which is above 7, so it is a base.

Incorrect: Black coffee (pH 5) is below 7, so it is a weak acid, not a base. Being closer to 7 makes it a weaker acid, not a base. Distilled water (pH 7) is neutral; lemon juice, with the lowest pH, is the most acidic. Baking soda solution (pH 9) is above 7, so it is a base; whether the number has one digit or two does not matter.

items.prompt: A lab technician has 200 mL of a salt solution with a concentration of 30 g/L. She adds 100 mL of pure water and stirs. What is the concentration of the new solution?
items.hint: Find how many grams of salt are in the original 200 mL. Adding water does not change the amount of salt, only the volume.
items.explain:
Salt in the original solution: 200 mL = 0.200 L, and 0.200 L × 30 g/L = 6 g of salt.

New volume: 200 mL + 100 mL = 300 mL = 0.300 L.

New concentration = 6 g ÷ 0.300 L = 20 g/L.

30 g/L assumes adding water does not change the concentration, but the same salt is now spread through more liquid. 15 g/L would be the result of doubling the volume (adding 200 mL), not adding 100 mL. 45 g/L multiplies instead of dividing; adding water can only lower the concentration.
